# Lesson Plan: Causes of the First World War

**Year 9 History | 50 minutes | 34 students**

## Learning Objective
Students will be able to identify and explain four long-term causes of WWI (Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism - MAIN) and explain how one short-term trigger (assassination of Franz Ferdinand) connected to them.

## Key Vocabulary (displayed on projector throughout)
Alliance, Militarism, Nationalism, Imperialism, Assassination, Trigger

---

## Lesson Sequence

### 1. Do Now / Retrieval (5 mins)
Projector shows a map of Europe in 1914 (no labels). Students write down, in silence, one country they recognise and one thing they already know about WWI. Cold-call 3 students for quick verbal answers. Low-stakes, gets everyone writing immediately.

### 2. Hook (5 mins)
Show a short (2-3 min) animated clip or projected image sequence of the "powder keg" cartoon (common in textbooks — a barrel of gunpowder labelled Europe with a lit match near it). Ask: **"Why might historians use this image to describe Europe in 1914?"** Take 2-3 hands-up answers. Introduce the lesson question: *Why did a war between so many countries start?*

### 3. Modelled Explanation - MAIN (10 mins)
Teacher-led explanation using the projector, one acronym letter at a time (Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism). For each:
- One simple sentence definition
- One visual (flag, ship, map of empires, soldier image)
- One-sentence example

Use consistent sentence structure each time: *"[Cause] made war more likely because..."* — this repetition supports weaker readers by giving a predictable pattern to latch onto.

### 4. Guided Practice with the Printed Sheet (15 mins)
**Distribute the single A4 sheet** (see below). Structure:
- **First 5 mins:** Whole class reads Section A together (choral/echo reading for the assassination narrative) — supports the six students with low reading ages by hearing it aloud before working independently.
- **Next 10 mins:** Students complete Section B (matching + fill-in-the-blank) independently or in pairs. Circulate, prioritising the six flagged students and any others struggling. Pair some weaker readers with stronger peers deliberately (pre-planned seating, not random).

### 5. Application Task (10 mins)
On the projector, display the question: **"Which MAIN cause do you think was most important? Why?"**
Students write 2-4 sentences in exercise books using a sentence starter (also on the sheet for those who need it):
*"I think the most important cause was ___ because ___. This links to the assassination because ___."*

Differentiation: higher attainers are pushed verbally to add a counter-argument ("However, some historians argue...") ; students needing more support may just complete the sentence starter with one clear reason.

### 6. Checking Understanding Before the Bell (5 mins)
**Exit method: Four-corners quick-fire + mini whiteboards (or scrap paper if no whiteboards available).**
- Teacher calls out four cause-cards one at a time: "Militarism," "Alliances," "Imperialism," "Nationalism."
- Students hold up scrap paper with a quick sketch/symbol they associate with it (ship, chain-link, flag, crown) — a low-literacy-friendly checkpoint.
- Follow with one rapid verbal question to the whole class: **"Shout out — what was the assassination that triggered the war?"** (Franz Ferdinand) — confirms the trigger-event link before dismissal.
- Teacher scans room during this for immediate misconceptions; no need for written collection given time constraint — this is a formative, in-the-moment check, and any gaps get addressed at the start of next lesson via a starter recap.

---

## The One Printed A4 Sheet (double-sided if needed, or single side with two columns)

**Title: Why Did WWI Begin? — MAIN Causes**

**Section A: The Spark**
*(Large, dyslexia-friendly font, short sentences, one image)*

> On 28th June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary was shot dead in Sarajevo. The killer was a Serbian nationalist called Gavrilo Princip. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia. Because of alliances, other countries were dragged in. Within weeks, most of Europe was at war.

**Section B: The Four Causes (MAIN)**
Simple table format, one row per cause, with:
- Cause name (bolded, large)
- A one-line definition with a **missing keyword** to fill in from a word bank at the bottom
- A tick-box matching column linking cause to a simple icon/example

| Cause | Definition (fill the gap) | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **M**ilitarism | Countries were building up their _______ and weapons. | 🚢 Navy race Britain vs Germany |
| **A**lliances | Countries made _______ promising to help each other in a war. | 🤝 Triple Entente / Triple Alliance |
| **I**mperialism | Countries competed for _______ around the world. | 🗺️ Colonies in Africa |
| **N**ationalism | People felt strong pride in their own _______. | 🏴 Serbian nationalism |

*Word bank: armies, promises, colonies, country*

**Section C: Sentence Starter for Your Answer**
> I think the most important cause was __________ because __________. This links to the assassination because __________.

---

## Notes on Inclusion
- The sheet uses large font, minimal text density, icons, and a fill-the-gap/word-bank structure rather than open writing — accessible for the six students with reading ages below 9 without singling them out (whole class uses the same sheet).
- Choral reading of Section A ensures those students access the narrative aurally before being asked to work with it visually.
- Seating pairs are pre-planned, not announced as "support," to avoid stigma.
